question: Can a model-free pipeline reconstruct sparsely visited separatrices by classifying basins, using predictive uncertainty to locate provisional boundaries, and generatively resampling those boundary regions?

key_findings.claim: The proposed pipeline turns basin labels into a generative sampler of approximate separatrix neighborhoods without requiring governing equations at inference.
key_findings.evidence: A dropout classifier maps initial conditions to basin labels, predictive entropy selects the highest-uncertainty points, and a score-based generative model learns their empirical distribution. The paper explicitly notes that the learned decision boundary is only a proxy whose validity depends on coverage, calibration, capacity, and class balance.

key_findings.claim: On the Newton fractal and CSTR examples, the score model reproduces the classifier-selected boundary distribution closely in low dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: For the Newton map, 40,000 labeled initial conditions train the classifier, 16,000 of 160,000 evaluation points train the score model, and generated versus selected samples have Chamfer distance 0.0115 and sliced Wasserstein distance 0.0493. For CSTR, the corresponding distances are 0.0088 and 0.0572.

key_findings.claim: Entropy-threshold stability can be measured rather than fixing the cutoff solely by convention.
key_findings.evidence: The CSTR analysis scans the 75th through 99th entropy percentiles and combines normalized point-count sensitivity with centroid-motion sensitivity. The lowest instability occurs at the 97th percentile, although the experiments retain the 90th percentile for a uniform demonstration protocol.

key_findings.claim: On the 3D Lorenz test, Monte Carlo dropout localizes the true stable manifold better than the tested ensemble and Laplace uncertainty methods, and the generative stage improves average coverage of that provisional boundary.
key_findings.evidence: Against a SCIGMA continuation manifold, the generated sample set reduces Chamfer distance from 3.05 for classifier uncertainty points to 1.58, raises coverage from 96.7% to 99%, and changes Hausdorff distance from 20.9 to 20.58. The paper reports MC dropout as best on coverage and Chamfer among the three uncertainty methods.

method.core_idea: Use epistemic uncertainty from a basin classifier as a data-driven boundary detector, then fit a score-based generator to produce dense samples near the detected separatrix.
method.mechanism: Uniformly sample initial conditions, obtain basin labels by long-time simulation, train a dropout neural classifier, run multiple stochastic forward passes to compute entropy, retain the top uncertainty percentile, and train a score-based generative model on those points. Optionally iterate by simulating generated candidates and use continuation-derived manifolds or dynamical diagnostics for validation.
assumptions: Basin membership can be labeled reliably from simulated or experimental trajectories even when equations are unavailable.
Training coverage is sufficiently uniform that high epistemic uncertainty mostly marks a basin boundary rather than an out-of-distribution hole.
The classifier is expressive and calibrated enough to approximate the desired boundary at the geometric scale of interest.
The score model reproducing the high-entropy distribution is useful even though that distribution may be a thick neighborhood rather than the zero-volume separatrix itself.
Class balance and entropy threshold are controlled so that the learned decision boundary is not systematically displaced.

techniques.role: Learns the global partition from initial conditions labeled by their asymptotic attractor.
Uses variation across stochastic classifier passes to identify provisional basin-boundary neighborhoods.
Fits a diffusion-style score model specifically to high-uncertainty points so new samples concentrate near the proxy manifold.
Balances sensitivity of selected-set size and centroid to choose a stable uncertainty percentile.
Uses SCIGMA stable-manifold continuation as an independent geometric reference for the Lorenz example.
Measures average coverage and worst-case deviation with Chamfer, sliced Wasserstein, coverage, and Hausdorff statistics.

evaluations.setting: Newton map z^3-1 on a 200x200 labeled grid, evaluated on 400x400 points
evaluations.metric: Chamfer and sliced Wasserstein distance between top-10% entropy points and 16,000 generated samples

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional non-isothermal CSTR with steady-state and limit-cycle basins
evaluations.metric: Threshold instability plus generated-versus-selected point-set distance
evaluations.result: 97th percentile minimizes instability; the fixed 90th-percentile demonstration yields 0.0088 Chamfer and 0.0572 Wasserstein
evaluations.baseline: Other entropy percentiles and the classifier-selected set

evaluations.setting: Lorenz system at sigma=10, rho=20, beta=8/3 with SCIGMA stable manifold
evaluations.metric: Coverage, Chamfer distance, and Hausdorff distance
evaluations.result: Generative refinement changes classifier-only values from 96.7% to 99% coverage, 3.05 to 1.58 Chamfer, and 20.9 to 20.58 Hausdorff
evaluations.baseline: MC-dropout high-uncertainty points before score-model refinement

evaluations.result: MC dropout is reported better than deep ensembles and Laplace approximation on coverage and Chamfer, and comparable or better on Hausdorff
evaluations.baseline: Deep ensemble averaging and Laplace approximation

limitations: Author-stated: sparse regions can produce false high-uncertainty islands far from a true separatrix.
Author-stated: finite smooth networks can erase fine or fractal boundary structure, and class imbalance can shift the decision boundary.
Author-stated: minimum data requirements, multi-seed robustness, active refinement, and better stopping or threshold criteria remain future work.
Reviewer-identified: Newton and CSTR metrics compare generated samples to the classifier's own high-entropy proxy, not to the true separatrix, so they mainly validate density imitation.
Reviewer-identified: only the 3D Lorenz case uses an independent continuation reference; no genuinely high-dimensional benchmark demonstrates the claimed scaling advantage.
Reviewer-identified: computational-efficiency advantages over continuation are asserted without wall-clock, simulation-count, or memory comparisons.
Reviewer-identified: uncertainty calibration, architectural details, random seeds, and score-model ablations are insufficiently reported for reproducibility.
failure_modes: Epistemic uncertainty rises in data holes, causing the generator to reinforce spurious boundaries.
A confident but wrong classifier can miss a true boundary entirely, leaving the score model no relevant training samples.
Fractal features below classifier resolution are smoothed away and cannot be recovered by generative resampling.
Class imbalance moves the learned boundary toward the minority basin.
A fixed percentile selects an overly thick band in one system and too few points in another.
Good mean Chamfer or coverage can coexist with large local holes, as the weak Hausdorff improvement on Lorenz indicates.
Generated points are not dynamically validated and may lie near the classifier boundary without lying near the true stable manifold.
reusable_insights: Separate boundary localization from boundary resampling: a discriminative model can find candidates while a generator improves coverage.
Uncertainty is ambiguous between boundary proximity and missing data; every active-boundary method needs an explicit disambiguation test.
Choose uncertainty thresholds using stability diagnostics and available simulation budget, not a universal percentile.
Validate learned manifolds with both average and worst-case distances and, where possible, an independent dynamical property.
Feed generated boundary candidates back to the simulator and relabel them before treating them as truth.
open_questions: Can iterative relabeling distinguish true separatrices from high-uncertainty data holes with finite simulation budgets?
What acquisition function best trades off global boundary discovery, local refinement, and basin class balance?
How does sample complexity scale with ambient dimension, intrinsic boundary dimension, curvature, and fractal dimension?
Can a generator target the zero-volume manifold directly instead of a threshold-dependent thick neighborhood?
Which dynamical tests—long transient time, saddle proximity, opposite outcomes under paired perturbations—provide reliable model-free validation?
Do calibrated ensembles or evidential classifiers outperform dropout after controlling compute and hyperparameter tuning?

competitive_landscape.title: On the approximation of basins of attraction using deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Shena et al. already formulate basin reconstruction as supervised classification and extract approximate basin boundaries, including a Lorenz example and basin-entropy analysis. This paper adds uncertainty-based candidate selection, score-based resampling, a threshold scan, and continuation comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: A Model-Free Sampling Method for Estimating Basins of Attraction Using Hybrid Active Learning (HAL)
competitive_landscape.difference: HAL actively exploits local basin boundaries and explores global ones while labeling informative experiments. The present pipeline begins with dense uniform samples and uses a score generator to reproduce uncertainty-selected boundary regions; its iterative active-learning version remains future work.

competitive_landscape.title: A Generative Adversarial Network for Climate Tipping Point Discovery (TIP-GAN)
competitive_landscape.difference: TIP-GAN adversarially generates model configurations that trigger a climate tipping point using an oracle and studies uncertainty near the tipping region. This paper targets state-space basin separatrices across generic multistable systems and uses classifier entropy followed by score-based manifold sampling.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Learning for Slow Manifolds and Bifurcation Diagrams
competitive_landscape.difference: Crabtree et al. use conditional score models to sample slow manifolds and fill bifurcation diagrams at requested quantities or parameters. The current paper applies related generative machinery to repelling basin boundaries, with a discriminative uncertainty stage supplying manifold samples.

competitive_landscape.title: Score-Based Generative Models Detect Manifolds
competitive_landscape.difference: Pidstrigach gives theoretical conditions under which score models produce the right manifold-supported kind of sample. This paper contributes an applied pipeline for acquiring separatrix-neighborhood training data, but does not derive analogous guarantees for noisy classifier-defined proxies.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is a systematic data-driven framework combining basin classification, uncertainty localization, and score-based generation for empirical reconstruction of separatrix manifolds without governing equations. Primary prior work already classifies and extracts basin boundaries, actively samples unknown basins, uses GANs around tipping points, and uses score models for slow manifolds and generic manifold support. Reviewer inference: the incremental novelty is the particular classifier-entropy-to-score-model composition, its low-dimensional demonstrations, and a Lorenz continuation comparison. The paper does not yet establish the claimed high-dimensional or computational advantage, and its planned iterative active-learning loop overlaps strongly with HAL.
reviewer_notes: Quantitative claims were checked on pages 5-11; the Lorenz continuation parameters appear in the page-10 footnote. The Newton and CSTR distances are explicitly proxy-distribution metrics, not direct true-boundary error. Competitive records and methodological differences were verified on primary arXiv pages.
